messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ahmad is a 78-year-old Middle Eastern man who has been working as a roofer for over five decades. His life took a dramatic turn several months ago when he was exposed to toxic chemicals during a renovation project. Since then, his world has become increasingly chaotic and frightening. On the day of the accident, Ahmad was at work on a large industrial building when a container of unknown chemicals ruptured, filling the air with a noxious gas. Despite his best efforts to evacuate quickly, he inhaled a significant amount of the toxic substance, leading to severe respiratory distress. The incident has left deep scars, both physical and psychological. Ahmad's symptoms have been especially pronounced around children, related news stories, and people connected to the accident. He often finds himself unable to relax even when he knows he is safe, as these triggers constantly remind him of that harrowing day. For instance, whenever Ahmad sees his own grandchildren playing in the park, a wave of panic surges through him, triggering vivid memories of the toxic fumes and his desperate attempts to escape. These involuntary recollections are often uncontrolled, intruding into his mind with alarming frequency. He finds it difficult to deliberately recall what happened but is overwhelmed by intense emotional responses without any clear visual memory. This fragmented experience of trauma haunts Ahmad whenever he encounters triggers like news reports or people from the workplace. Each time a trigger surfaces, such as seeing children or hearing someone from work, his memories force their way into his mind unbidden, filling him with dread and anxiety. Ahmad’s startle response has become exaggerated since the incident. A simple touch can set off an intense alarm in him, leaving him feeling vulnerable and on edge. This heightened state of alertness makes it hard for him to fall asleep or stay asleep at night, further exacerbating his distress. Ahmad is certain that any small disturbance could remind him of the accident and trigger another wave of anxiety. The cycle has become increasingly self-reinforcing over time. His fear of unexpected touches amplifies his general sense of threat, which in turn makes it harder for him to relax even when he knows he’s safe. This continuous state of hypervigilance has begun to interfere with his daily life and work as a roofer. Ahmad often finds himself avoiding social interactions or news that might trigger memories of the accident. Ahmad’s wife, noticing these changes in her husband, encouraged him to seek help after months of deteriorating quality of life. She noted how he would react violently at unexpected touches during their daily routines and would frequently wake up in the middle of the night drenched in sweat. What frightens Ahmad most is the fear that he will never be able to live normally again without being haunted by those memories. Ahmad is seeking help now, hoping for a way to regain control over his life and find peace from the relentless intrusions of his traumatic experiences. He hopes to learn how to manage these triggers so that he can continue working as a roofer and enjoy time with his family without constant fear.
